idiom_name: duck-typed no-op class + stdlib precedents (logging.NullHandler, contextlib.nullcontext)
implementation_notes: Python has neither interfaces nor a null-safe reference type - None is a value, not a collaborator - so the pattern is realized by a small class that implements the same protocol methods and does nothing, installed as the default (def __init__(self, logger=None): self.logger = logger if logger is not None else NullLogger()). The standard library ships working precedents: logging.NullHandler is 'essentially a no-op handler for use by library developers', and contextlib.nullcontext() returns enter_result from __enter__() but otherwise does nothing. Prefer None with an explicit 'is None' check (or dict.get, getattr(obj, name, default)) when absence is meaningful; use the null object when the code must call unconditionally.
pitfalls: 'logger or NullLogger()' misfires for falsey-but-valid collaborators (a strategy or collection with __bool__/__len__); compare with 'is None' instead.

A duck-typed null object that omits a method fails only when that method is first called, and only on the null path - the path least exercised in production; implement the whole protocol (or subclass abc.ABC / typing.Protocol) so the omission fails early.
unittest.mock.Mock() is not a null object: it accepts every call and records it, so a misspelled method silently passes instead of doing nothing visibly.
